blogs.title: From Bark to Blood: Spotting Capnocytophaga canimorsus in the ED
blogs.description: Why a familiar dog bite can mask a rare but deadly pathogen. Explore Capnocytophaga’s epidemiology, the pitfalls of slow‑growing cultures, early clinical clues of sepsis and DIC, and why empiric coverage for fastidious gram‑negative rods can change a patient’s trajectory.

blogs.title: Between DIC and TMA: How Sepsis‑Triggered Coagulopathy Can Hide Microvascular Thrombosis
blogs.description: When a septic patient’s labs scream DIC yet a new drop in hemoglobin and schistocytes appear, what are you looking for? A detailed look at overlapping laboratory findings, the importance of peripheral smear interpretation, and the diagnostic cascade that separates consumptive coagulopathy from emerging TMA in the ICU.

blogs.title: CM‑HUS or TTP? A Practical Algorithm for the Acute Adult TMA
blogs.description: TTP and CM‑HUS share MAHA and thrombocytopenia but diverge clinically and therapeutically. Learn how to apply the PLASMIC score, interpret ADAMTS13 activity, use complement panels, and decide when to start plasma exchange versus eculizumab.

blogs.title: Complement Inhibition Amid Bacteremia: When to Turn the Switch on Eculizumab
blogs.description: Balancing the life‑saving benefits of eculizumab against its risk of compromising defense against encapsulated organisms. This post discusses timing relative to culture clearance, vaccination strategies, antibiotic prophylaxis, and real‑world evidence from CM‑HUS secondary to C. canimorsus.

blogs.title: Plasma Exchange in CM‑HUS: That Temporary Help or the Core Treatment?
blogs.description: Is PEX a bridge or a mainstay in complement‑mediated HUS? We review the literature, mechanisms of action in the context of infection‑triggered complement dysregulation, and clinical decision‑making regarding duration and sequencing with complement blockade.

blogs.title: When Genomics Fails the Tests: Understanding the Hidden ‘Second Hit’ in CM‑HUS
blogs.description: Many CM‑HUS patients have no identifiable complement gene mutation. This article delves into the concept of a second, often infectious, trigger, why a negative panel may not guarantee safety, and the implications for treatment duration and family counseling.
